Bunker Hill. On June 17, 1775, American militia fortified Breed's Hill overlooking Boston Harbor, though the location became known by its neighboring landmark. British Commander William Howe attacked with frontal assaults, and the Americans, short on ammunition, inflicted staggering casualties before being forced to retreat. The Americans were commanded by Israel Putnam, who issued the famous order: don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes. British forces made three costly uphill charges to overrun the American entrenchments. British casualties were over 1,000, representing 40 percent of their force. American losses were approximately 450, with many surrounded or out of ammunition. Though technically a British victory, the heavy losses boosted colonial morale and proved American regulars could stand against professional troops. Occurred in June of 1775, three months after Lexington and Concord and before the Declaration of Independence, this battle demonstrated that colonial militia could inflict real damage on the world's premier military power, shaking British confidence in an easy victory.
